title: Still the best sunrise in the country
content: I have been four times now and the moment the towers come out of the dark over the pool still gets me. We stood on the left side of the northern pool, which was less crowded than the right. Go back at three in the afternoon: the galleries were almost empty and the Churning of the Sea of Milk had nobody in front of it.

title: Worth the 4:30 alarm
content: Bought the three-day pass the evening before so we could go straight in at five. The sunrise crowd is real, hundreds of phones, but once the sun is up most people leave for breakfast and you can walk the bas-reliefs in peace. The climb to the upper level has a queue by nine; I went at seven and walked straight up. Bring a scarf for your shoulders.

title: Magnificent, but plan for the heat
content: The scale is hard to describe until you walk the causeway with two children asking how far it is. The carvings of the Battle of Kurukshetra kept my son interested for twenty minutes, which is a record. We made the mistake of staying until eleven; by then the stone radiates heat. A good guide is worth the money here more than anywhere else.

title: Architecture that explains everything after it
content: We came here on our first morning and everything else at Angkor made sense afterwards. The proportions of the five towers, the way the galleries step up, the perfect symmetry of the moat. Our guide explained that the temple faces west, which is why the sunrise is behind it and why the best light on the facade is actually late afternoon. He was right.

title: Spectacular, crowded, unmissable
content: Nothing prepares you for how big it is. We went at sunrise with what felt like half of Siem Reap, then had breakfast at the stalls outside and came back in at eight when the groups had moved on to Bayon. The apsara carvings along the walls are extraordinary. My mother found the steps to the upper level steep, so we skipped that and were still happy.

title: Faces in every direction at four o'clock
content: For photographs this is the temple. Midday is flat and harsh, but from about half past three the sun comes in low from the west and the faces on the eastern towers get their shadows back. I spent an hour on the upper terrace moving between towers as the light changed. The bas-relief of the Cham naval battle on the east side is lit beautifully in the morning instead.

title: Our king's smile, two hundred times
content: I bring my guests here after Angkor Wat and tell them to look for the market scenes on the outer gallery: women selling fish, a cockfight, a man cooking on a brazier. It is daily life from eight hundred years ago and it looks like Siem Reap market this morning. Then we go up to the faces. Everybody goes quiet. That is why I love this temple.

title: Beautiful but tight at the top
content: The upper terrace is small and by ten there were tour groups blocking every good angle. We waited twenty minutes for a clear shot of the famous nose-to-nose faces. Still, when you stand in the middle and realise every tower is looking at you, it is unlike anywhere else. Go early or late, not in the middle of the morning like we did.

title: The most human temple at Angkor
content: The faces have been argued over for a century, Lokesvara or Jayavarman himself, and standing among them I decided it does not matter. What moved me was the outer gallery: soldiers marching, a woman giving birth, a man being bitten by a turtle. The Khmer who carved this wanted to be remembered as people, not just as a kingdom. Allow more time than you think.

title: Dense, detailed, half under scaffolding
content: A fascinating building, more complex than Angkor Wat in some ways, with 37 of the original 54 towers still standing. Part of the inner gallery was under restoration when we visited, with scaffolding on two towers, which spoiled the best views and took the shine off the visit for us. The reliefs are extraordinary and poorly labelled; take a guidebook. We cycled here from town in forty minutes and parked at the south gate.

title: The trees won, and good for them
content: Yes, it is the Tomb Raider temple, and yes, there is a queue for the famous root. Ignore both. Walk the one-way route slowly at eight in the morning and the place is silent apart from the cicadas and the odd falling leaf. The combination of collapsed galleries and enormous silk-cotton roots is like nothing I have seen. The restoration work is tactful.

title: Beautiful but very busy by ten
content: I came with friends from university at nine and by the time we reached the central enclosure the walkway was a queue. The roots are amazing, especially the one that pours over the gallery wall like water. The wooden walkways make it easy to get around. Next time I will come at opening or in the last hour before closing, as everyone advised us.

title: Quiet in the late afternoon
content: I went at four when most tours had gone and had long stretches of the route to myself. The light through the canopy was green and soft. I sat on a fallen lintel for twenty minutes and watched a tree root that must have taken two hundred years to reach the ground. Thank you to the Indian conservation team for leaving it like this.

title: The finest carving we saw in Cambodia
content: A jewel. Everything here is small and everything is carved, down to the smallest pilaster. The pediment of Ravana shaking Mount Kailasa is as good as anything in a European cathedral. We arrived at seven thirty, before the buses, and had the inner enclosure almost alone for twenty minutes. The pink sandstone glows in early light. Combine with Kbal Spean as we did.

title: A scholar's temple, not a king's
content: The temple was commissioned by a Brahmin counsellor, which perhaps explains the refinement: there is no bombast here, only craft. The guardian figures kneeling before the libraries, the Indra on his elephant, the dancing Shiva. I read for years about this place and it was better. The visitor centre is good and the walk around the moat afterwards is peaceful.

title: Exquisite, and small enough for teenagers
content: After three days of enormous temples our two teenagers had reached their limit. This was the right antidote: tiny, intensely detailed and done in forty minutes. The carvings really are astonishing, and the pink stone photographs well even at midday. The drive out through the villages was part of the pleasure. The Landmine Museum on the way back made a strong impression on the kids.

title: A forest pyramid all to ourselves
content: Rode out from Siem Reap on the motorbikes, three hours with a stop at Beng Mealea, and arrived at Prasat Thom at noon with nobody else there. Climbing the wooden stairs to the top of a seven-tier Khmer pyramid with the forest stretching to the horizon was the high point of the whole trip. Prasat Pram with its tree-wrapped towers is five minutes away. Carry water; there is little shade.

title: Remote, impressive, poorly signposted
content: A long day from Siem Reap but worthwhile. The pyramid is unlike anything else in Cambodia and the view from the top is superb. The rest of the site is scattered over several kilometres and the signage is minimal, so a driver who knows the temples is essential. The entry fee is separate from the Angkor pass. The new UNESCO status does not seem to have brought crowds yet.

title: Good stop between Phnom Penh and Siem Reap
content: I break the drive here when I take clients north. Forty minutes off the road, brick towers in light forest, a guide from the village who speaks good English. The octagonal towers are unusual and the carved flying palaces are worth looking for. It is not Angkor and does not try to be. Quiet, shaded, well kept since the UNESCO listing.

title: Where Khmer architecture starts
content: Three centuries before Angkor, and you can see the vocabulary forming: the tower shape, the lintels, the lions at Prasat Tao. Walking between the three groups in the forest with a local guide took us two hours and I would happily have taken four. Almost no visitors on a weekday in December. The small museum at the entrance is modest but useful. Deeply satisfying.

title: Our palace, still beautiful
content: We take every visiting relative here and it never disappoints. The Throne Hall roof in morning sun, the Silver Pagoda floor, the little iron pavilion from Napoleon III that looks like it landed from another planet. Go at eight when it opens; by ten the tour buses have arrived. Remember it closes over lunch. Dress properly or you will be turned back at the gate.

title: Grand, hot, closed at midday
content: Very impressive buildings and the Silver Pagoda is extraordinary, though you shuffle through it in a line. Our mistake was arriving at eleven, when it closes for two hours, so we had to come back. The gardens are immaculate and there is some shade. Children under a certain height were free. Allow ninety minutes and bring water.

title: Different from our palace, equally serene
content: As a Thai visitor I kept comparing it to the Grand Palace in Bangkok, and the differences were the interesting part: quieter, greener, less gilded, with the same Buddhist calm at the centre. The Emerald Buddha in the Silver Pagoda is a smaller, more intimate cousin of ours. The guards were polite about the dress code. A peaceful hour in a loud city.

title: Beautiful, but you are herded a bit
content: Gorgeous roofs, gold everywhere, and a real sense that the king is just behind the wall. The downside is the route: you follow a fixed path and the Silver Pagoda is a slow queue with no photos allowed inside. Still worth it. We went in the late afternoon slot and the light on the Throne Hall was the best of the day.

title: A calm morning before meetings
content: I had two hours free before a client meeting and spent them here. Ten minutes from the hotel on foot, open at eight, almost empty for the first half hour. The Silver Pagoda alone justified the ticket. The staff were helpful about the dress code and had sarongs available. One of the few places in Phnom Penh where you cannot hear traffic.

title: See the statues first, then the temples
content: The best advice I give anyone going to Angkor is to come here first. The great Jayavarman VII head, the Harihara, the reclining Vishnu bronze from the West Mebon, all explained and lit properly. The building itself, Groslier's red pavilions around the lotus courtyard, is as lovely as anything inside. Two hours flew by. The audio guide is worth every riel.

title: Beautiful courtyard, uneven labels
content: The collection is wonderful and the courtyard garden with its ponds is the calmest place I found in Phnom Penh. Some of the labelling is thin, so the audio guide helps. No photography inside the galleries, which I respected but regretted. The café in the courtyard served a good iced coffee and I stayed longer than planned.

title: The hardest ride and the best view
content: Six of us rode up from Sra Em and took the motorbike taxis for the final steep section, which is not for the nervous. Then you walk the whole length of the temple, gate after gate, climbing, until the cliff drops away in front of you and all of Cambodia is spread out five hundred metres below. Windy, silent, extraordinary. Check the border situation before you go; the soldiers were friendly but present.

title: A pilgrimage, in every sense
content: Getting there is half the point: a long drive from Siem Reap, a night in Sra Em, a pickup up the mountain. The temple is a sequence of gopuras along a ridge, each more ruined and more beautiful than the last, and the final terrace on the cliff edge is genuinely breathtaking. Facilities are basic. We were lucky with access; it depends on the politics.

title: Twenty minutes well spent on the road north
content: Every driver on the Phnom Penh to Siem Reap road passes this and almost nobody stops. We did. A laterite bridge from the twelfth century with naga balustrades and twenty-one arches, and lorries used it until a few years ago. Walk down to the riverbank to see the arches. The sticky rice sold at the stalls is good too. A quick, worthwhile stop.

title: An empire read from its bridges
content: We hired a driver who knew the old road east and spent a day stopping at bridges and the ruins of rest houses between Beng Mealea and Bakan. Spean Ta Ong, a laterite bridge nearly eighty metres long, was the highlight. There are no signs and no tickets, only the road and the forest. For anyone who has read about the Khmer road network, a quiet thrill.

title: Rough track, enormous reward
content: Two hours of dirt track from the main road on the bikes in the dry season, and then a temple enclosure so large you cannot see one side from the other. Collapsed towers, a face tower reflected in a pond, the hospital chapel almost intact, and not another visitor all day. Looted and unrestored, which somehow makes it more moving. Take water, food and a guide who knows the way.

title: Hear it before you see it
content: We came in September when the rains were still on, and the sound reached us from the car park. The second tier is enormous in the wet season, a brown wall of water throwing spray up to the viewing platform. The steps down were slippery and worth it. Dry season people say it is better for swimming; wet season is better for being amazed. Go on a weekday to avoid the picnic crowds.

title: Impressive falls, long day from town
content: An hour from Sen Monorom on a sealed road, so easier than we expected. The two tiers are spectacular and the zipline over the gorge was good fun for the price. The area at the top is a bit built up with stalls and shelters, which takes something from it, but once you go down the steps to the lower fall it is wild again. Good photos everywhere.

title: Elephants on their own terms
content: No riding, no bathing, no selfies with trunks. We walked with the mahouts through the forest and watched the elephants do what they wanted, which was mostly eat and scratch against trees. Our teenagers, who had been cynical, were silent for an hour. The guides explained the history of each animal and the Bunong communities the project supports. Book ahead; numbers are capped.

title: The only ethical elephant visit I found
content: I researched for weeks before choosing this and I am glad I did. A full day of walking steep forest trails, watching retired working elephants forage in the valley, lunch at the base, and a long talk about why the project refuses to let visitors touch the animals. It is not cheap but the money goes to the forest and the villages. Wear proper shoes; the paths are muddy.

title: A perfect green circle
content: Fifteen minutes from Banlung and you are swimming in a volcano. The water is clear and cool, the forest comes right down to the rim, and the walk around the lake takes about an hour at a slow pace. We went early on a weekday and had the eastern pier to ourselves. The Tampuan cultural centre on the trail is small but worth ten minutes. The fee goes to the village, which is how it should be.

title: Lovely swim, busy on Sunday
content: A genuinely beautiful crater lake with clean water and a well-kept trail around it. We made the mistake of going on Sunday afternoon, when every family in Banlung had the same idea and the piers were full of children and speakers. Still a good swim. Weekday mornings are clearly the time. The changing huts are basic but adequate.

title: Houses in the sky, boats at the door
content: We visited in late November when the lake was still high and the boats tied up at the front steps of houses ten metres off the ground. The children loved the small paddle boat through the flooded forest, rowed by a woman from the village who pointed out kingfishers. Sunset over the open lake from the boat was perfect. Buy the ticket at the community office, not from touts.

title: Striking, with a touch of the tour circuit
content: The stilt houses are extraordinary and the flooded forest paddle is magical. The slightly uncomfortable side is the number of boats doing exactly the same loop at the same hour, and the inevitable stop at a floating shop. Go late afternoon, tip the woman who rows you through the trees, and stay out for the sunset. Better than the Chong Kneas alternative by a long way.

title: A different Cambodia from the temples
content: After three days of stone it was good to see something alive. Fish drying on racks, children paddling home from school in boats, a pagoda on stilts. Our boatman was patient with my parents and the flooded forest was calm and beautiful. The afternoon heat on the open water was fierce, so take hats. The sunset made up for everything.

title: The children talk about it still
content: We took our two kids on a Sunday afternoon and it was the hit of the year. A bamboo platform, a lawnmower engine, rice fields flying past at what feels like a hundred kilometres an hour and is probably thirty. When another car came the other way everyone jumped off and lifted ours off the rails. The village at the end sells drinks and bracelets. Pure joy for five dollars.

title: Silliest and best thing we did
content: Four grown men on a bamboo bed on wheels, rattling through the countryside laughing the whole way. The driver let one of us sit at the back by the engine. Yes, it is a tourist thing now and the original line has moved, but who cares. Go in the late afternoon when the light on the rice is golden and the heat has gone.

title: Fun ride, no longer the real thing
content: The ride itself is enjoyable, twenty minutes each way through pleasant countryside. What you should know is that this is a purpose-built track near Banan rather than the original working line, and the far end is a row of stalls built for visitors. Treat it as a theme ride and you will enjoy it. The drivers were cheerful and the price was fair.

title: My home town by bicycle
content: I grew up in Kampong Cham and had never cycled the trail until a colleague visited. We crossed the bamboo bridge to Koh Paen, rode through the rubber trees and stopped at Wat Nokor on the way back. The bridge is rebuilt each dry season and wobbles beautifully. Start early, the island roads have no shade after nine. Hire bikes on the riverfront.

title: Where our country began
content: Every Khmer should come here once. The reclining Buddha carved into the top of a boulder, the river of a thousand lingas under clear water, and the waterfall where families picnic and children swim. The road is one way up before eleven and down after noon, so plan for the whole day. The ticket is separate from the Angkor pass. Weekends are full of local families, which I like.

title: Sacred mountain, busy waterfall
content: The carvings in the riverbed were the highlight for me: hundreds of lingas under running water, carved a thousand years ago to bless the river that feeds Angkor. The waterfall below is beautiful but crowded on weekends with picnics and loud speakers. The reclining Buddha at the summit was peaceful. Worth the extra ticket, but go on a weekday if you can.

title: A swim after the temples
content: We did this on our last day and it was the right choice: a mountain, a waterfall and a swim after a week of stone. The road up is steep and one way, so our driver timed it carefully. The pool under the big fall was cold and wonderful. The riverbed carvings are easy to miss unless someone points them out. Bring a towel and food.

title: Cold air and clouds, an hour from home
content: We ride up from Kampot whenever friends visit. The road is good now, the temperature drops as you climb and by the top you want a jacket. The old church in the mist, the restored palace hotel, the giant statue of Lok Yeay Mao, and then the cloud comes in and swallows everything. Popokvil waterfall is small but pretty. Leave by four before the fog thickens.

title: Eerie, atmospheric, oddly developed
content: The ghost town feel is real when the cloud rolls through the old church and the colonial ruins. What nobody tells you is how much new construction there is on the plateau: a casino, apartment blocks, wide empty boulevards. It is a strange mix of abandoned and half built, and it left us a little cold. The views over the coast when the mist clears are superb. Take a car rather than a scooter; the weather changes fast.

title: Ruins in the clouds
content: The old Bokor Palace has been restored, which is a pity in one sense and a relief in another; the church and the smaller ruins keep the melancholy. We arrived at two in sunshine and by three could not see twenty metres. Wat Sampov Pram on the cliff edge, with its rock shaped like a boat, was the most beautiful stop. Bring a jacket, really.

title: A road trip that felt like another country
content: Rented scooters in Kampot and rode the thirty kilometres up. Pine trees, cold air, fog, and this abandoned church that looked like Scotland. Then a casino out of nowhere. We ate noodles at the top wrapped in hoodies. The viewpoints over the gulf when the cloud lifted were incredible. One of the best days of the trip. Fuel up before you start the climb.

title: Good day trip from the coast
content: We drove over from Sihanoukville for the day. The plateau is cool and green and the old buildings are atmospheric, especially the church. The giant statue is impressive if a little new. Weekends bring a lot of Khmer families up for picnics, which makes it lively. The waterfall had little water in March. The road is excellent and the views on the way up are the best part.

title: The best birding morning of my life
content: We left Siem Reap at half past four, crossed the lake as the sun rose and were in the flooded forest by seven. Thousands of painted storks, spot-billed pelicans on every tree, darters, openbills, a grey-headed fish eagle. From the ranger platform you look across treetops full of nests. It is a long and expensive day and I would do it again tomorrow. January is the month.

title: Long lens, early boat
content: I went with a conservation operator in February. The light in the first hour on the water was pink and still and the birds were everywhere. The platforms put you at nest height, which is extraordinary for photographs. You need a long lens and a hat; there is no shade on the lake crossing. The floating village of Prek Toal itself is worth the walk at lunch.

title: Different from October to April
content: We came in April when the lake was low and walked under the houses on their tall stilts, which is strange after seeing photos of boats at the same doors. The village is a real working place: nets, shrimp farms, a school. The boat ride to the open lake was short because the water had retreated so far, and it felt like half a visit. Go at the end of the rains if you want the flooded forest.

title: The lake town visitors miss
content: I take guests here instead of Chong Kneas whenever they have time. Fifty kilometres from town, a working fishing town of thousands, houses ten metres high, and maybe four other foreigners all afternoon. Fish smoking on racks, boats being built, children waving from windows. The afternoon light on the water is the best on the lake. Allow half a day.

title: Bats, a million of them, every evening
content: We go up the hill with visitors for the pagoda and the views over the rice plain, and then we wait at the bottom at six. The bats start as a trickle and become a river that pours out of the cliff for half an hour, twisting over the fields. My children count them and give up. The killing caves on the way up are a sombre reminder; take a moment there.

title: Heavy history, then the bats
content: The caves where the Khmer Rouge killed people are a hard visit and should be. The pagoda at the top has a huge view and a lot of monkeys. Then at dusk we sat on the roadside with everyone else and watched the bats stream out of the cliff for forty minutes. Incredible. Hire a moto up the hill unless you enjoy steep roads in the heat.

title: Our town's quiet pride
content: Battambang does not shout about itself, but the galleries behind the old shophouses on the river are some of the best in the country. Walk the three riverside streets in the late afternoon when they open, have a coffee, and if Phare has a show that night, go. The circus school is the heart of it. The shophouse facades alone are worth the walk.

title: The best colonial streetscape in Cambodia
content: The shophouses along the Sangker are better preserved than anything in Phnom Penh, and the galleries inside them are small and serious. We saw a painting show at a riverside gallery and a sculpture studio open to the street. The Phare circus performance in the evening was superb: energetic, funny, moving. The town itself is slow in the best way.

title: Still my favourite island
content: I grew up on the coast and Koh Rong is where we go when we want to forget the town. Long Set beach is wide and empty by eleven when the day-trippers have moved on, the water is clear and shallow for a hundred metres, and at night we swam with the plankton lighting up around our arms. Koh Touch is loud; walk twenty minutes east and it is gone.

title: The glowing water is real
content: We were sceptical about the bioluminescence and then at ten at night on Long Set beach we waved our hands under the water and it lit up blue. Unreal. Daytime was beaches, a boat trip to Sok San on the west coast, and too much grilled fish. The ferry was easy from Sihanoukville, forty-five minutes. Bring cash; the ATM was out of service.

title: Paradise, with a plastic problem
content: The beaches on the west coast are the most beautiful I saw in South-East Asia, seven kilometres of white sand with nobody on them. Honesty requires saying that the village end has rubbish issues and the party strip at Koh Touch is grim at night. Walk away from it and the island is extraordinary. I stayed four nights and would have stayed longer.

title: Quieter than Thai islands, which is the point
content: Compared with Koh Samui or Phuket this is twenty years back in time: few roads, generator electricity in places, beaches with nothing on them. That is exactly why I came for a long weekend. The snorkelling off the north was decent, the sunset from the west coast superb. Ferries stop in bad weather, so leave a buffer before your flight.

title: Long weekend done right
content: Five of us from the office, three nights, a bungalow on the beach, a boat to the sunset side, fish on the grill every evening. We hired a longtail for a day and visited three beaches with nobody on them. The island is bigger than people think and the best parts take effort to reach. Worth every hour on the bus from Phnom Penh.

title: Worth the ridiculous price, once
content: We saved for this and it delivered: an overwater villa with the reef under the deck, staff who remembered everything, and the knowledge that a chunk of the bill funds the marine reserve and the village across the channel. Snorkelling at dawn off the house reef, dinner on the sand, a massage in a pavilion over the sea. It is an anniversary place, not a holiday place.

title: Lovely, remote, very expensive
content: A beautiful resort on two tiny islands with a footbridge between them. The villas and food are faultless and the conservation story is sincere. Two small points: the speedboat transfer is long and bumpy in any wind, and there is nothing to do beyond the resort, which suits some people and not others. We enjoyed two nights; a week would have been too much for us.

title: Not what it was
content: I used to come to Otres every month when it was a row of little beach bars with hammocks and cheap fish. Most of that was bulldozed in 2020 and the sand now sits in front of fenced plots and half-finished buildings. The water is still calm and the sunset is still straight ahead, but the life has gone. Go for a swim and a sunset drink at one of the few places left, nothing more.

title: A calm beach for a family afternoon
content: We knew nothing of what it used to be, so we simply found a long quiet beach with shallow water, casuarina shade and a couple of restaurants. The children swam for hours and we kayaked for one. Compared with the town beaches it is clean and peaceful. The sunset was lovely. We would come back.

title: Crab and pepper, nothing else needed
content: We drove down from Phnom Penh for one lunch and it was worth the three hours each way. You pick your crabs from the basket in the water, agree a price per kilo, and ten minutes later they arrive stir-fried with whole strands of green Kampot pepper. We ate two kilos between four of us, with grilled squid on the side. Then a walk along the shore past the old villas. Perfect.

title: The best meal of the trip
content: Blue swimmer crab with fresh green pepper is one of the great dishes of South-East Asia and this is where to eat it: on a wooden deck over the water, watching women pull the next baskets from the sea. We paid eleven dollars a kilo. The ruined French villas along the coast road and the old resort feel of Kep made it a whole afternoon.

title: Our weekend ritual
content: From Kampot it is forty minutes on the motorbike, so we come for sunset most months. Watching the crabs lifted from the baskets never gets old, and the prices are the same for Khmer and foreigners if you buy at the market stalls rather than letting a restaurant choose for you. Grilled squid with lime and salt, a beer, the sea turning orange. Simple and perfect.

title: Fresh, fair, fun
content: A proper working market with restaurants attached, which is what I hoped for. The crab with green pepper was excellent and the prices were posted. It gets crowded with Phnom Penh families on Sundays and parking is chaos. Weekday lunch was calm. The pepper is different from anything in Thailand, floral and sharp. I bought a kilo of dried to take home.

title: Messy, delicious, memorable
content: Our teenagers were sceptical about cracking crabs with their hands and then ate more than we did. The stilt restaurants behind the market are all much the same; we picked one with a sea view and were happy. Agree the price before they cook. The walk along the shore afterwards to see the ruined villas and the national park trail above made it a full day.

title: Home, and best at six o'clock
content: I am biased, I live here. But watch a visitor on the riverside at sunset when the Bokor ridge goes pink behind the old bridge and they understand. The shophouses are restored, the night market behind is good for cheap food, and the sunset boats are worth the few dollars. Then fireflies on the way back. Kampot does not hurry and does not need to.

title: A town that lets you slow down
content: I planned two nights and stayed five. Mornings cycling along the river, afternoons reading in a riverside café, evenings watching the mountain change colour. The old French shophouses and the mismatched spans of the Old Bridge give it a gentle, faded beauty. The sunset cruise with fireflies afterwards was the most peaceful hour of my trip.

title: A good base, a pleasant walk
content: Kampot works as a base for the pepper farms, the caves, Bokor and Kep, and the riverfront is a pleasant place to end each day. The restored shophouses are attractive and the river is wide and slow. It has become a long-stay expat town, with the pros and cons that brings, and a little too comfortable for our taste. The sunset boat was good value; the firefly stretch upriver was the highlight.

title: Taste it green off the vine
content: The farm tour was free and the guide was a young woman from the village who knew everything. We walked under the shade netting between four-metre poles of vines, learned the four colours, and tasted a fresh green peppercorn straight from the plant, which is a small explosion. Then the shop, where I bought far too much. The red soil, the hills of Kep behind. Lovely morning.

title: Interesting and well organised
content: I buy Kampot pepper for a restaurant client in Saigon so this was partly business. The farms around Damnak Kantuot are well set up for visitors, with short tours, tastings and clear explanations of the geographical indication. Harvest season in March was busy with sorting. Prices at the farm are better than in the city. The road from Kampot takes half an hour by tuk-tuk.

title: Pretty farm, good photos, great pepper
content: The rows of vines under palm-leaf shade are beautiful and very photogenic in the morning light. The tour was short and friendly and the tasting was fun, especially the red pepper. We combined it with the Secret Lake and the cave at Phnom Chhnork in a half day by tuk-tuk. The shop is the end of every tour, naturally. We left with three bags.

title: Five days, no roads, gibbons at dawn
content: The trek to the Veal Thom grasslands was the hardest and best thing I did in Cambodia. Kavet guides, river crossings up to the waist, hammocks under tarps, gibbons calling at first light and the grassland plateau opening out on day three. Everything was arranged through the park office in Banlung and nothing felt improvised. Fitness required; leeches in the wetter weeks.

title: The locals' waterfall
content: Half an hour from Sen Monorom on red dirt, no crowds, two small falls in the forest and a deep green pool under the second one. We swam for an hour in February and had it to ourselves apart from a family picnicking. In the rainy season the water goes brown and fast and you would not swim. Much smaller than Bou Sra and much calmer.

title: Birds on the sandbars at first light
content: We hired a boat on the Stung Treng riverfront at half past five and ran upriver to where the Sesan and the Srepok meet. Wide braided water, sandbars with river terns and lapwings, fishing villages waking up on both banks. The dam downstream has changed the river and the boatman talked about it honestly. A quiet, beautiful morning that few travellers bother with.

title: Red soil, cool mornings, honest coffee
content: A café in Sen Monorom arranged a morning on a Bunong family's coffee plot. We walked among the bushes, saw cherries drying on tarpaulins and drank a cup roasted the day before while the mist lifted off the hills. The Sea Forest viewpoint afterwards, hills folding away forever, was the view of the trip. Cambodia's coffee deserves more attention than it gets.

title: An afternoon that becomes a night
content: Five minutes on the ferry from Kratie and the island slows you down immediately. We cycled the nine-kilometre loop through pomelo orchards and two villages, stopped at the pagoda, and watched the sun set behind Kratie across the water. Then we stayed the night at a community homestay and ate with the family. Buy pomelos from the roadside; they are the best in the country.

title: A gentle cycle and a floating village
content: The flat loop road is easy for anyone and the island is pretty: gardens, wooden houses, a little floating Vietnamese community at the southern end where I spoke my own language for an hour. The sandbar in the dry season is good for a swim. Kratie itself has little to do, so this is the thing to do. Bicycles are at the ferry landing.

title: We saw six and the children were silent
content: Our boatman cut the engine as soon as the first fin appeared, and for an hour we drifted while the dolphins surfaced around us, sometimes thirty metres away, once much closer. The children, who are never silent, were silent. Go early morning or late afternoon as everyone says. The boat was nine dollars a person. Phnom Sambok on the way back has a good view.

title: Too many boats, too few dolphins
content: We went at eleven in the morning, which was our mistake, and there were seven boats circling the pool. We saw two brief fins in an hour. Some of the other boats kept their engines running, which cannot help. The river itself is beautiful and the boatman was kind, but the experience felt like it was pushing the animals. Early morning, fewer people, probably different.

title: Pines and a jacket, two hours from town
content: The Phnom Penh escape. We camped on the plateau in December, woke to mist in the pines and needed jackets until nine. The cliff viewpoint over the Elephant Mountains, the old royal villa ruins in the trees, a waterfall swim at Chambok. It fills on Saturday nights with city families and speakers, so go Sunday to Monday if you can. Take warm clothes, really.

title: Cool air for the kids
content: We went for a day from Kandal and the children loved the pine forest, which looks nothing like the rest of the country. Cycling on the plateau roads was easy and cool. The resort at the top is pricey for lunch, so we brought a picnic. The viewpoint is a short walk and worth it. Weekends are busy with families like us.

title: A tiny temple inside a mountain
content: Two hundred steps up a limestone hill in the rice fields outside Kampot, and inside the cave a brick shrine from the seventh century with a stalactite growing down to meet it. The schoolboys who guide you for a tip know every rock shape and every bat. Twenty minutes, a dollar or two, and one of the stranger sights in the province. Go early before the heat.

title: Wide river, wide falls, quiet forest
content: I came across the border from Trat for two nights. The boat from the Tatai bridge up to the falls takes twenty minutes through mangrove and rainforest, and the falls are a broad shelf of rock with the whole river coming over it. In March the flow was modest and the pools below were good for swimming. Lodges on the river arrange kayaks. Peaceful and uncrowded.

title: Three days, one leech, no regrets
content: A friend and I did a three-day trek out of Thma Bang with a community guide: river crossings, a night in hammocks by a stream, hornbills overhead, elephant dung on the trail and a long climb to a ridge where the forest went on in every direction. It is the wildest country left in Cambodia and it feels like it. Dry season only, and go with proper guides.

title: Saracen Bay by day, Lazy Beach at sunset
content: The quiet island. Saracen Bay is a long white crescent with shallow warm water and no music, and the jungle path across to Lazy Beach takes half an hour and ends with the sun setting into the open sea. We did the walk three evenings running. The plankton glows here too, on the dark nights. Electricity and signal are patchy; that is part of it.

title: The quiet I was looking for
content: No roads, no engines after dark, a bay of white sand and a path through the forest to a beach facing the sunset. I read, swam and walked for four days and spoke to perhaps ten people. M'Pai Bay at the north end has a small village and cheap food. The ferry from Sihanoukville was straightforward. Take cash and a torch.

title: Beautiful, a bit sleepy for a group
content: Gorgeous bay, clear water, decent snorkelling off the south end from a boat trip. For four friends it was almost too quiet; one night of silence is bliss, three is a lot. The jungle walk to Sunset Beach was a highlight and the plankton swim was unforgettable. If you want nightlife go to Koh Rong; if you want the opposite, this.

title: The clearest water I have dived in Cambodia
content: A two-night liveaboard from Sihanoukville, four hours out to Koh Tang and Koh Prins. Visibility of twenty-five metres, healthy coral, big schools of fusiliers, nudibranchs everywhere and a reef shark on the second dive. The island's war history was told respectfully by the crew. Long hours at sea, basic bunks, and absolutely worth it for anyone who dives. Calm season only.

title: Walkway, tower, then the boat
content: The concrete walkway through the mangrove is easy with children and the tower at the end gives a wide view over the channels to the islands. The better part was the boat afterwards at high tide, gliding between roots with kingfishers and egrets everywhere. We did not see the dolphins, which the guide warned us was likely. A good half day from Koh Kong town.

title: Nice river trip, worrying development
content: The boat down the mangrove river from the park headquarters was pleasant: macaques in the trees, kingfishers, a sea eagle, and a quiet beach at the end for a swim. What troubled us was how much of the park on the drive in has been fenced and cleared for construction. The river itself still feels protected. Go for the boat and manage your expectations.

title: Six o'clock on the quay
content: After work half the city comes down here: aerobics groups with speakers, families with children on scooters, couples on the wall, old men feeding the pigeons at the shrine. Buy a sugar-cane juice, walk north from the palace and watch the light go orange over the Mekong. The one-hour boat trips at dusk are cheap and worth it. Watch your phone in the crowd.

title: Best walked an hour before sunset
content: I stay on the quay for work and the evening walk is my routine. The river junction is wide and handsome, the palace roofs catch the last light, and the whole promenade becomes a public living room. It is noisy and the street food is hit and miss, but the energy is real. During the Water Festival in November it is a different, much wilder place.

title: Look up before you shop
content: I have shopped here since I was a child and I still stop under the dome to look up. Gold and jewellery in the centre, clothes and electronics in the arms, flowers and fruit at the back, and a food hall for lunch. It is hot by eleven; the dome ventilation works best early. Prices for visitors start high but come down quickly with a smile.

title: Art Deco at its most useful
content: As an architecture lover this was my favourite building in Phnom Penh: a 1937 dome of extraordinary lightness, with the yellow lattice windows throwing patterns on the gold counters below. The restoration was done with care. We bought nothing but a krama and a coffee and spent an hour simply looking. Go early, before the heat and the crowds.

title: Everything, for everyone, under one roof
content: Clothes for the children, silk scarves for my mother, a bag of Kampot pepper, a tiny Buddha carved from wood. The aisles are narrow and hot and I loved it. The food stalls in the corner did a very good vegetarian noodle soup once I explained. The cafés in the streets around the market were a cool reward afterwards. Go in the morning.

title: Bargains and a sauna
content: Factory overruns of brands you know at a fraction of the price, plus silver, scarves, spare parts and a food corner that smells incredible. It is the hottest place in Phnom Penh by midday; we were dripping within twenty minutes and lasted forty before giving up. Haggle gently, it is expected. The coffee shops in the neighbourhood afterwards are some of the best in the city.

title: Good for a family evening
content: We walked from the Old Market through the night market lanes with the kids: scarves, paintings, silver, fried ice cream rolls, a bag of fried crickets that nobody finished. Pub Street next door is loud but fun to walk through once. The massage places are cheap. The riverside walk home under the lanterns was the best part. Prices need bargaining.

title: Fun once, then it is the same stalls
content: Lively, cheap, and every stall sells the same scarves and elephant trousers. Pub Street is exactly what it sounds like: cheap beer, loud music, good for one night with friends. The food lane in the market was decent, especially the grilled skewers. After two evenings we were done. The riverside walk home was nicer than the market itself.

title: The city laid out like a map
content: We went up for sunset on our last night and it was the right way to end. The glass terrace hangs out from the tower with the river junction and the palace roofs below, and the city lights come on while you watch. Cocktails were twenty dollars and excellent. Smart casual means it: a man in sandals was politely turned away. Book a terrace table.

title: Great view, not our kind of place
content: Three of us rode up to Phnom Penh and wanted to see the famous view. We got the view, which is genuinely amazing, and a drink that cost what we spend on dinner for three. One friend was refused entry for shorts and waited downstairs. Staff were polite, the place is beautiful, but for the price I would rather be on the riverside with a cold Angkor.

title: An afternoon of good coffee and old tiles
content: I spent a whole afternoon walking between cafés in Boeng Keng Kang: a roaster in a 1960s villa with original floor tiles, a tiny pour-over bar, and a street corner where an old man dripped coffee through a cloth filter over ice with condensed milk. The Cambodian beans from Mondulkiri were better than I expected. A quiet way to see the city.

title: Breakfast at seven, gone by nine
content: We got to Psar Leu at seven and found the noodle sellers with their pots and baskets of herbs. Soft rice noodles, green fish gravy, banana blossom and a heap of mint, eaten on a plastic stool for a dollar. My husband had the red version. By nine the women were packing up. If you want to understand Khmer food, start here, not at a restaurant.

title: They made it vegetarian without fuss
content: I told them in advance we were vegetarian and the whole menu was adapted: tofu amok steamed in banana leaf, a mushroom lok lak, green mango salad and pumpkin custard. The market hour at the start was the best part, learning the herbs and the pastes. We pounded kroeung in stone mortars until our arms ached. The recipes came home with us and we have used them.

title: Fun morning, great photos, good lunch
content: A half-day class with a market tour first, then six of us around a long table making fish amok, beef lok lak and a mango salad. The teacher was funny and patient. The amok we steamed ourselves in banana-leaf cups was genuinely good, and we ate everything. A bit touristy in the sense that every school does the same menu, but that menu is what you want to learn.

title: Watch a man climb a palm before breakfast
content: My uncle's village makes sugar and we took the children at dawn in December. A man climbed a thirty-metre palm on a bamboo ladder with a knife and bamboo tubes, came down with the sap, and his wife boiled it for hours in wide pans over a fire of fronds. The children stirred. The warm syrup on sticky rice is the best thing I know. You will never buy pale factory sugar again.

title: Khmer food taken seriously
content: We had dinner in the courtyard by the water with the traffic of Norodom Boulevard somewhere far behind the walls. Prahok ktis with crisp vegetables, Kampot pepper crab, a fish amok that made every other amok we had eaten seem a rough sketch, and a palm-sugar dessert. Service was warm and unhurried. Not cheap by Cambodian standards and worth every dollar.

title: The model that works
content: I spent four nights in Chi Phat and it is the best community tourism I have seen anywhere. You book at the village office, the guides are former loggers who know the forest better than anyone, the money is shared and visible in the school and the clinic. I did a two-day trek to a waterfall and the jar burial site, and a day of mountain biking. Boat in from Andoung Tuek for the river.

title: Mountain bikes, bat caves and a homestay
content: Rode in on the dirt road from the highway, which is rough but fine in the dry season. The community office sorted a homestay, a guide and bikes within half an hour. A day of riding to a waterfall and a bat cave, dinner with the family, frogs all night. The village is simple and real. Next time I will do the multi-day trek.

title: Face towers, a thousand arms, and nobody there
content: I stayed a night in the village homestay and walked into the temple at dawn with mist still on the moat. Face towers like Bayon, collapsed galleries, and the two surviving reliefs of the many-armed Avalokiteshvara, which alone justify the long drive from Sisophon. Not another visitor all morning. The community group runs everything well; dinner with the host family was the finest meal of the week.

title: A half day the children enjoyed
content: Tuk-tuk from the city, a little ferry across the Mekong, then bicycles along lanes between vegetable plots and wooden houses with looms clacking underneath. The weavers let the children try the shuttle. The silk centre near the ferry explained the process. In the dry season there is a sandy beach at the north end with huts. An easy, pleasant escape from the traffic.

title: Best course in the country, play at dawn
content: A seven o'clock tee time, mist on the fairways and the clubhouse coffee afterwards made for a very good morning between meetings in Siem Reap. The Faldo layout is fair and well kept, the greens were quick, the caddies excellent. By eleven the heat is brutal, as everyone warns. Green fees are international, as is the standard. Clubs for hire were decent.

title: Calm pool, honest drivers, good breakfast
content: We had the family suite for four nights. The two rooms with a shared balcony worked well for us and the children lived in the pool between temple visits. The house tuk-tuk drivers charged fixed prices and were waiting at five for sunrise without being asked twice. Breakfast had both Khmer noodle soup and eggs. Wifi was slow in the evenings; otherwise no complaints.

title: The right size of hotel
content: Twenty-four rooms, which means the front desk knows your name by the second morning. My deluxe room had a proper desk, strong air-conditioning and a balcony over the frangipani. The free airport pickup arrived on time, the restaurant's amok was better than most in town, and the lane is quiet at night despite being ten minutes from the market. I would stay again for work or pleasure.

title: Our own house in Siem Reap
content: Four of us took the two-bedroom villa for a week and barely wanted to leave. A pool to ourselves, a housekeeper who laid out mangoes and coffee each morning, a cook who came in twice for dinners on the terrace that beat any restaurant we tried. The driver handled the temple days. Wat Damnak is leafy and silent after ten. Expensive for Cambodia, cheap for what it is.

title: Pod beds that actually let you sleep
content: The female dorm on the top floor was the best hostel bed I had in Asia: a curtain, a light, two sockets, a locker that took my whole pack, and a balcony over the river. The rooftop was sociable without being a party, and it really did go quiet at eleven. The shared kitchen was clean. Breakfast is paid and basic; the noodle carts outside are better.

title: Great rooftop, bad night
content: The rooftop and the location are as good as everyone says. Our night was not. The air-conditioning in the eight-bed dorm failed around midnight and nobody could fix it until morning, so we slept in a sauna. The next day the shower on our floor had no hot water. Staff were apologetic and moved us for the second night, which was fine. Ask for the top floor.

title: Dark skies and the sound of the stream
content: I came for the night sky and got it: no light for kilometres, the Milky Way over the thatched roofs, and the stream below the veranda all night. The bungalows are simple, fan and net, solar hot water that worked. In the morning a guide from the village walked us up to the river carvings before any day-trippers arrived. Dinner over charcoal was excellent. Bring a torch.

title: The children saw a hornbill from the veranda
content: The family lodge at the end of the path gave us two rooms, a wide veranda and a hornbill on the second morning. The walks with the village guide were pitched well for teenagers. Two honest notes: there is no air-conditioning and April afternoons were hot, and the drive from Siem Reap is long. Both are the point of the place. Food was simple and very good.

title: My guests thank me for this one
content: As a guide I look for homestays that are really homes, and the Chea family's house is one. Guests sleep upstairs behind the family rooms, eat what the family eats, and go into the flooded forest at dawn in the family boat before the tour boats. Everyone comes back talking about the grandmother. Basic bathroom, shared, downstairs. That is the deal and it is a good one.

title: The quietest morning of my trip
content: I woke at five to the sound of a paddle and watched the family's boat come back with the night's catch. Then we went out together into the drowned forest with the mist still on the water and the egrets waking up. The room was a mattress and a net and a window onto the lake, and that was enough. Dinner on the floor with the family was the best meal I had.

title: Everything a business trip needs
content: Fast check-in, a quiet river-view room with a real desk, a gym open at six, and a breakfast buffet that covered Khmer, Japanese and Western tastes. The executive lounge was useful for a late meeting over coffee. Twenty minutes to the airport as promised. The rooftop pool at sunset is a bonus I used twice. Priced like a five-star and behaves like one.

title: Grand, comfortable, a little formal
content: Our executive suite was large and silent despite the quay below, and the children loved the rooftop pool. Breakfast was excellent and the concierge arranged a palace guide at short notice. It is a formal hotel; the children felt they had to whisper in the lobby. The Chinese-speaking staff were a help for my parents. Good value for the category.

title: Like staying with an aunt
content: A villa with mango trees, a fan room for eighteen dollars and Mrs Sok making noodle soup to order. The family gave me a hand-drawn map of the neighbourhood's cafés and I used every one. Bicycles are free. The fan room gets warm in the afternoon, but I was out by then anyway. A ten-minute walk to the Russian Market. Honest and kind.

title: Good value, good people, thin walls
content: A well-run family guesthouse in a quiet street with a lovely garden for breakfast. The air-con double upstairs was clean, the shower hot, the wifi adequate. The walls are thin and the room next door had an early riser. Mr Sok's restaurant tips were spot on, and the bicycles saved us tuk-tuk fares all week. Fair price for what you get.

title: A proper apartment for a working month
content: I stayed four weeks in a one-bedroom residence and it solved every small problem of a long trip: a kitchen with an oven, a washer-dryer, a desk with a view, housekeeping twice a week. The 28th-floor pool before breakfast was my routine. The coworking lounge printed my contracts. Walking distance to the riverside and the banks. The weekly rate made sense against any hotel.

title: Looms at dawn, river at night
content: I sat with Mrs Rath at the loom for a morning and managed a few centimetres of plain silk that she kindly called good. The riverside bungalow was simple and perfect, with a hammock facing the Mekong and boats passing all day. Dinner was cooked on the bank and eaten with the family. The city is forty minutes away and felt like another country.

title: Sleeping between the pepper rows
content: We had a hillside bungalow with a bathtub by the window and a daybed facing the Kep hills. Mornings started with the farm walk, learning the four colours, and the restaurant's green-pepper crab at dinner was as good as the Kep market's. The spring pool under the mango trees was cold and lovely. The shuttle to Kampot ran on time. Our best two nights of the trip.

title: A farm stay done with style
content: Comfortable bungalows, a very good kitchen that uses the estate's pepper intelligently, and a genuinely working farm around you. The red-pepper ice cream is worth ordering. Minor points: the bungalows are close enough to hear neighbours on their verandas, and the road in is rough after rain. Bicycles to the Secret Lake and the cave at Phnom Chhnork made a fine afternoon.

title: The roof is the reason
content: Friends from Phnom Penh stayed here and I joined them on the roof every evening: Bokor turning pink, cold beer, the river below. Rooms are plain and clean and the river-view balcony rooms are worth the extra ten dollars. The desk sorted their motorbikes and the sunset boat without fuss. Breakfast downstairs is simple. Exactly what a guesthouse should be.

title: Cheap, central, motorbikes sorted
content: Three of us took two rooms for twenty dollars each and spent the days on the Bokor road and the pepper farms. The guesthouse rented us decent bikes with helmets and a map, and the rooftop at sunset was where every evening ended. Hot showers worked. The fan rooms at the back are quieter than the river rooms if you are an early sleeper.

title: Crab at seven, pool by nine
content: Three families shared the five-bedroom villa for a long weekend and it was the easiest holiday we have had. The chef came back from the crab market each morning with the day's plan and cooked for twelve without fuss. The pool on the rocks, the boat to Rabbit Island, kayaks for the children, a night guard so we slept. Expensive, and split twelve ways it was not.

title: Low, quiet and on the sand
content: A resort that kept itself small: two-storey wings, villas with plunge pools on the beach, and a spa under the casuarinas where I had the best massage of the trip. The adults-only pool was empty most afternoons. Dinner on the sand by candlelight, kayaks at dawn, staff who remembered how we took our coffee. It is the calm end of a coast that is otherwise being built over.

title: Lovely resort, strange surroundings
content: The resort itself is excellent: good rooms, good food, a beautiful stretch of beach kept spotless. What you cannot ignore is the empty cleared land and half-built towers you drive past to reach it, and the construction noise some mornings from the north. Inside the gates it is a bubble. If you can live with the contrast you will have a good stay.

title: Sixteen bungalows and the whole sunset
content: Thirty minutes by boat from the pier and you are on seven kilometres of beach with sixteen bungalows and nothing else. Our beachfront bungalow had a hammock, an outdoor shower and the water ten steps away. The restaurant grilled fish from the village boats every night. The kayaks and snorkels were free. Power ran all night. The office group has already booked again.

title: Beautiful, basic, no wifi to speak of
content: If you need to be connected, this is not your place, and that is a compliment. Fans and nets instead of air-conditioning, a shower heated by the sun, a deck facing west. The sunset from the restaurant tables was the best of our trip and the staff took us out for the plankton after dinner. Boats back to Koh Touch run three times a day, so plan around them.

title: Barefoot and offline
content: A longhouse dorm, six huts on the sand, a kitchen we cooked in and a bar with cold beer. No roads, no signal, no air-conditioning, and a glowing sea at night. The hostel's boat met us at Saracen Bay so we did not have to carry packs over the jungle path. Two nights was perfect for us; three would have been too quiet. Bring cash and a torch.

title: My kind of hostel
content: I usually avoid hostels and loved this one. A private beach hut with a double bed and a hammock for twenty-four dollars, a dorm longhouse for those who want it, a shelf of swapped books and a shared kitchen where strangers cooked together. The sunset is straight out front. The water was cold in the shared bathroom and nobody minded. Quiet by ten.

title: Our town's prettiest house to sleep in
content: My husband and I stayed a night as a treat while the children were with their grandparents, and the balcony suite over the river was worth it: four-metre ceilings, the original tiles, a clawfoot tub and the long balcony where we watched the river traffic with a glass of wine. Breakfast in the courtyard café was good. The family who run it know everyone in the art quarter.

title: Teak shutters and tiled light
content: A photographer's house: morning light through the teak shutters onto 1920s tiles, a long balcony over the river road, the courtyard café downstairs. My heritage double at the back was quiet and cool. The free bicycles took me to Phnom Sampeau for the bats and back. The only drawback was street noise early on the front rooms, which mine avoided.

title: A fireplace in Cambodia
content: We came up in January and the lodge had its fireplace going, which I had never seen in this country. Pine bungalows with thick duvets and a hot shower that mattered at eight hundred metres. The shuttle took us to Bou Sra and the elephants, and the Bunong guide's forest walk was the best morning. Food was good, portions generous. The view down the valley at dawn is the reason to come.

title: Plain, clean, and the river at the window
content: I stay here when work takes me to Kratie. Nothing fancy: a tiled room, cold air-conditioning, a hot shower and a balcony on the Mekong with the island opposite. Breakfast on the terrace with the river traffic is the pleasure. The desk books the dolphin boats and the minivans at local prices without being asked. The lift works, which in Kratie is a point.

title: The easy way into Ratanakiri
content: A garden of jackfruit and cashew trees, wooden bungalows with hammocks, and owners who sorted a motorbike, a map and a Virachey trek through the park office within an hour of our arrival. The bungalow was simple and clean with a hot shower. Breakfast under the trees with strong Ratanakiri coffee. Ten minutes to the crater lake. The red dust is unavoidable.

title: Floating on the edge of the forest
content: A floating bungalow with a ladder straight into the river, a kayak tied to the deck and nothing but forest on the far bank. The boat to the waterfall was twenty minutes, the swim below the falls cold and clean, and dinner on the floating platform was by candlelight with fireflies in the trees behind. Composting toilets and solar power, done well. Worth the detour from Koh Kong.

title: Reliable Khmer food off the noisy street
content: When friends visit and want amok near Pub Street, this is where I take them. The amok is set properly, not soupy, the lok lak dip is sharp with lime and pepper, and the balcony lets you watch the street without being in it. It is not cheap by Siem Reap standards and the ground floor is loud. Upstairs, with a jug of draught, it is a good evening.

title: They made it mild for the children
content: We asked for the children's curry without chilli and it came that way, which does not always happen. Fish amok, chicken samlor korko, a huge plate of fried rice, and the red ants with beef for the adults, which the children found hilarious. Picture menu, high chairs, quick service, air-conditioning downstairs. For a family after a day of temples, exactly right.

title: Where the drivers eat before your sunrise
content: Every guide in Siem Reap knows Mrs Sophal's cart. We stop at half past five on the way to Angkor Wat, the guests eat kuy teav on plastic stools with the tuk-tuk drivers, and they understand the day differently afterwards. The broth is clear and deep from pork bones simmered all night. A dollar fifty. Sold out by ten. This is Siem Reap.

title: The brunch I measure others by
content: Cold brew from Mondulkiri beans, eggs on good sourdough, and a courtyard that stays shaded until noon. I edit photos here most weeks. The staff tolerate laptops until the lunch rush and the wifi is quick. The pumpkin and coconut soup is the best thing on the menu and nobody orders it. Weekend mornings mean a short wait. Worth it.

title: Vegetarian breakfast done properly
content: Granola with fruit and yoghurt, avocado on sourdough, a very good flat white with oat milk and a vegan cake that my daughter approved. After a week of pointing at menus and asking about fish sauce, this was a relief. Prices are closer to Europe than Cambodia. The courtyard is lovely in the morning. Service was friendly and quick.

title: Lake fish for groups, at local prices
content: On the way back from Kampong Phluk I bring groups here for a late lunch. Order for the table: fish amok, sour soup with lotus stem, grilled snakehead with lime and salt, fried fish with green mango. Tin roof, fans, long tables, a fraction of the Pub Street price. It is not pretty. The amok is as good as any in town. Ask for prahok if you are brave.

title: Two dollars of cold fruit
content: A mango and passion fruit smoothie with ice and nothing else, blended while I watched, for two dollars, on the corner of the Old Market. The two sisters who run it have the same prices for everyone, which is rare on that corner. A young coconut opened with a cleaver on the way back from the night market. Nothing more to say; go.

title: The bowl every driver pulls in for
content: On the Banteay Srei road every tuk-tuk stops at Preah Dak and most stop at Yeay Phan's stall. The noodles are pressed each dawn, the green gravy is thin and fragrant, and the herbs are piled on without asking. A dollar a bowl. I have brought a hundred guests here and the only complaint was that it was gone by afternoon. Eat before the temple, not after.

title: Better than any in Phnom Penh
content: I grew up eating num banh chok and I say this carefully: the Preah Dak version is softer and more sour than ours and the gravy is lighter. We ate two bowls each at eight in the morning before Banteay Srei and bought sticky-rice sweets for the car. The women were amused that a Phnom Penh family had come so far for noodles. Worth it.

title: Friday night as it should be
content: Eight of us from the office, two braziers, plates of marinated beef, pork belly, squid and prawns, morning glory in the broth around the grill, and jugs of draught with ice. Loud, smoky, cheap, and the staff kept the coals going without being asked. We smelled of charcoal until Saturday and nobody minded. Book a table on Fridays.

title: An hour's wait and the wrong bill
content: I brought two clients here on a Saturday because it had been recommended. We waited an hour for a table with a reservation, the coals arrived cold and had to be relit twice, half the order came wrong, and the bill included plates we never received. Correcting it took twenty minutes and an argument. The food, when it came, was fine. Not an evening I will repeat.

title: Khmer flavours, small plates, good wine
content: The best new thing in Bassac Lane. Kampot pepper squid, pork belly glazed with palm sugar, a prahok dip that converted a friend who swore she hated prahok, and a glass of something natural and orange from the wine list. Twenty stools at the counter, a courtyard under a tamarind tree, a DJ on Saturday that did not drown conversation. Book for weekends.

title: Bai sach chrouk the way it should be
content: Thin slices of pork marinated in coconut and garlic, grilled over charcoal before dawn, over broken rice with pickles and a bowl of clear broth. This is the Phnom Penh breakfast and the stalls on the ground floor of Orussey do it best. Steel tables, market noise, prices in riel, done by ten. Take a seat where there is one. My father has eaten here for thirty years.

title: Serious coffee behind the market
content: The roaster runs in the window most mornings and the whole lane smells of it. I take a pour-over of whichever Mondulkiri lot is on and a bag of beans for the office. The slow-drip iced coffee with condensed milk is there for the traditionalists and it is good. Small, a little hard to find, worth it. The Saturday cupping is free.

title: Dinner that changed my view of Khmer food
content: I took a client who thought Khmer cooking was Thai without the chilli. Seven courses later he had changed his mind: banana blossom salad with smoked fish, duck in samlor kari, Kampot lobster in green pepper, slow beef saraman, palm-sugar custard. Each dish explained at the table, the wine pairing well judged, the villa and garden beautiful. Expensive and worth it.

title: Refined, careful, slightly hushed
content: The tasting menu is a scholarly tour of the refined Khmer table, with recipes that I had only read about in old cookbooks. The saraman was the finest I have eaten. My only reservation is the atmosphere: the room is so quiet that one feels one should whisper, which is not how Khmer food is meant to be eaten. Still, a remarkable evening.

title: Sunset, pepper margarita, band
content: A fourth-floor roof over the quay with the river junction in front of you. We went up at half past five for the sunset and happy hour, stayed for the beef skewers and the band, and came down at midnight. The pepper margarita is better than it sounds. Prices are tourist prices, as expected. Book a rail table or you will stand.

title: A good place to take visiting colleagues
content: The view over the Chaktomuk at dusk is the best way to show a first-time visitor what Phnom Penh is. Cocktails are competent, the grilled fish for sharing was good, service was quick despite a full terrace. Music gets loud after nine. Smart casual is relaxed here, unlike the tower bar across town. We stayed two hours and left happy.

title: Warm baguettes twice a day
content: The baker trained in Lyon and it shows: a real crust, a soft inside, and croissants that go by nine. We buy a pâté baguette for lunch and a passion-fruit tart for the afternoon, and sit under the tamarind trees on the quietest street in town. The coffee is fine rather than special. Order whole cakes a day ahead; the lemon one is excellent.

title: Our Friday crab
content: The crabs sit in baskets in the river until you order, so they are alive ten minutes before they reach the wok. Stir-fried with whole strands of green pepper from the family's farm, with rice and a mountain of napkins, on a deck over the river with the mountain going pink. Prawns in tamarind on the side. Prices by the kilo, fair. We come most Fridays.

title: Crab, beer, sunset, repeat
content: After the Bokor ride we came straight here, filthy and starving, and were treated well anyway. A kilo of crab in green pepper between three of us, grilled squid, clams with basil, a lot of cold beer and the sun going down behind the ridge. Slightly slow service when the deck filled up. Worth the wait every time.

title: Skewers and grilled bananas for the children
content: We let the children loose at the night market with a few dollars each and they came back from Bong Vuthy's grill with pork skewers and sticky chicken wings, then from his wife's cart with grilled bananas in coconut caramel. Everyone ate standing by the river wall. Cheap, cheerful, sold out of wings by nine. Cash and KHQR only.

title: Choose your crab from the basket
content: We drove down from Battambang for a family weekend and ate here twice. You pick the crabs from the basket in the shallows, agree the kilo price, and they come back six ways; the green pepper is best but the salted egg version surprised us. The floor is planks over the water and the children watched fish through the gaps. Sunset over Rabbit Island at the table.

title: Wonderful for crab, thin for vegetarians
content: My husband and children said the crab was the best of the trip and I believe them. For a vegetarian the choice was fried rice, a vegetable stir-fry and morning glory, all competent, all incidental. The setting over the water is beautiful and the staff were kind about it. Go for the seafood; bring a vegetarian only if they are patient.

title: Coffee under the vines before the trail
content: We stopped here before walking the Kep National Park loop and again after. A good espresso, a pepper hot chocolate that works, and a passion-fruit cheesecake that was the best thing I ate in Kep apart from crab. The garden terrace is shaded and the shop sold me pepper and sea salt packed for the flight. Closed on Tuesdays, which we learned the hard way.

title: Fried rice while the norry turns around
content: The canteen at the end of the line is a thatched shelter with a wok and a dozen tables, run by a farming family. Fried rice with egg, morning glory with garlic, grilled chicken with lime, and a cold coconut hacked open at the table, all in the few minutes before the car goes back. Nothing is written down. The children loved pointing at the wok.

title: Our town's best table
content: A 1920s shophouse on the river with its tiles intact and paintings from the galleries next door on the walls. The duck confit with green Kampot pepper is the dish, the beef saraman with baguette a close second, and the palm-sugar tart finished us. The two-course lunch set is a bargain for office workers like us. Closed Mondays. Book for Friday dinner.

title: The last beach bar standing, and the best
content: Tables on the sand that move back with the tide, the day's fish on a bed of ice priced by weight, and a charcoal grill that turns a snapper into dinner in fifteen minutes. We had barracuda with Kampot pepper butter and tiger prawns with chilli-lime, happy hour cocktails and the sun going down straight in front. Lanterns and music after dark. It is what Otres was.

title: The chalkboard changes with the boat
content: A fishing family's house with a dozen tables under thatch at the quiet end of Koh Touch. The father catches, the mother and daughters cook. We had a whole grilled grouper with lime and salt and a sour soup with pineapple, rice, papaya salad and beer from a chest of ice. Cash only; when the fish is gone they close. Simple and exactly right.

title: Three pots at dawn
content: Om Srey's cart under the tamarind trees by the Koh Trong ferry is where Kratie starts its day. I had the beef noodle soup with its dark star-anise broth, my colleague the kuy teav, and we watched the sun come up over the island while the ferry workers ate around us. A dollar a bowl, iced coffee from the next cart. Gone by ten.

title: Bunong coffee, roasted behind the counter
content: A Bunong farmer and his wife buy ripe cherries from their neighbours and roast them three mornings a week in a small drum behind the bar. The pour-over of a single farm's lot was the best coffee I have had in Cambodia, and the slow-drip iced coffee kept the locals happy. We did their farm tour the next morning and the cupping at the end. Buy beans here, not in Phnom Penh.

title: Home town fish, done right
content: The fish comes off the boats at the landing beside the tables: trey ros, trey pra, snakehead, rubbed with turmeric and lemongrass and grilled whole until the skin blisters. Eaten with herbs, rice and a tamarind dip under the riverside trees while the lights come on along the bamboo bridge. Ribs glazed with palm sugar for the children. Beer in towers for the adults.

title: Wetland fish and prahok by the jar
content: We drove down from Kandal at five to see the boats come in from Angkor Borei with the night's catch: snakehead, eels, the giant freshwater prawns Takeo is known for. My mother bought prahok from a clay jar in three grades. Then grilled fish on bamboo with rice and herbs on a stool by the water for two dollars. Winds down by noon.

title: The capitals in order, which changes everything
content: I followed the trail over nine days with a driver: Sambor Prei Kuk first, then Koh Ker, then Angkor, then down to the palace in Phnom Penh. Seeing the brick towers before the sandstone pyramid before Angkor Wat makes the whole story legible in a way the usual Siem Reap circuit never did. The budget range in the trail notes was accurate. Long drives, but the sequence is the point.

title: Ambitious for a family, rewarding anyway
content: We did a shortened version in six days with the children: Angkor for three, Sambor Prei Kuk on the drive south, then Phnom Penh for the palace and the museum. The route notes helped us order the days and the museum at the end tied it together for the kids. Full version would need stamina. Hotels along the way were easy to find.

title: The river as a road
content: From the floating villages of the Tonle Sap to the silk island near the capital, then up the Mekong to the dolphins at Kampi and the trail villages around Kampong Cham. I did it in eight days, partly by boat, partly by bicycle, partly in the office truck. Life on the water links the whole thing and the route makes that visible. Koh Trong at sunset was the high point.

title: Pepper, crab, islands, in that order
content: We drove the coast route over a long holiday: Kampot for the pepper farms and the river, Kep for the crab market, then the ferry to Koh Rong Sanloem for three nights. The order works and the distances are short. The budget estimate held except for the island, where everything costs more. The children rank the crab market first and the plankton second.

title: A good week off the Saigon flight
content: Flying into Phnom Penh and driving straight to the coast made a sensible week: Kampot, Kep, Koh Rong Sanloem, back via Bokor. The corridor description is honest about what each stop is. I would have liked a day more in Kampot and a day less on the island, but that is taste. Roads are good; the ferry schedule needs checking in the wet season.

title: Forest first, plateau last
content: Four of us from Siem Reap took a week off and followed the mountain route: Kirirom for a night in the pines, Chi Phat for two days of trekking and kayaking, Tatai for the waterfall, and Bokor to finish in the clouds. The order is right, the budget is realistic if you stay in homestays, and the roads were better than I expected. Dry season only.

title: Eating the country from north to south
content: A cooking class and the noodle markets in Siem Reap, a palm-sugar farm in Kampong Speu, a grill night in Phnom Penh, then the pepper farms and the crab market on the coast. The trail is really a shopping list of the Khmer kitchen and following it in order makes sense of the flavours. Ten days was generous; a week would do. Come hungry and buy an extra bag.
